name: Object Pool
intent: Keep a limited set of expensive objects ready, lend them out, and take them back for reuse instead of creating a new one each time.
scenario: A server talks to a database that allows only a few connections. Opening a connection is slow, and many requests arrive at the same moment.
problem: Each request opens its own connection and closes it afterwards. Opening is slow, and a burst of requests opens more connections than the database allows, so some requests are refused.
solution: A Pool creates a fixed number of connections on demand and keeps them. A request calls acquire() to borrow one and release() to give it back. The pool resets the connection before lending it again. When all are in use, the next request waits for a free one instead of opening another, so the limit holds.
pain: Every request pays the cost of opening a connection
A burst opens more connections than the database allows
Requests are refused instead of waiting for a turn
Connections are opened and closed all day
benefits: Objects are created once and reused
The number of live objects has a hard upper limit
Extra requests wait in line instead of failing
Reset on return keeps one borrower's state from leaking into the next
whenToUse: Creating an object is slow or uses a scarce resource, such as a connection or a thread
The other side allows only a limited number of them
Requests come in bursts and each one uses the object for a short time
whenNotToUse: Objects that are cheap to create: the pool costs more than it saves
Objects that cannot be reset to a clean state safely
When the platform already pools them for you, as many database drivers and ORMs do (ADO.NET, SQLAlchemy, most Java connection pools)
pitfalls: Leaks: a code path that does not release the object slowly drains the pool until every request waits forever
Returning an object without resetting it leaks one borrower's state to the next
A pool that is too small makes requests queue, and one that is too big overloads the other side
Waiting without a timeout turns a full pool into a hung service

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Borrows an object with acquire(), uses it briefly and gives it back with release().

roles.label: Pool
roles.description: Creates objects up to a limit, lends free ones, takes them back and resets them.

roles.label: Pooled object
roles.description: The expensive object being shared, such as a database connection.

roles.label: Factory
roles.description: Knows how to create a new pooled object when the pool needs one.

quiz.question: A database allows 100 connections. An app opens one per request, and in a burst of 300 requests 200 of them fail with a too-many-connections error. What is the best change?
options: Use a connection pool with a fixed size, so that extra requests wait for a free connection
Raise the database limit to 1,000 connections so that bursts of this size fit in
Retry each failed request straight away until the database accepts a new connection
Close each connection later, so that fewer connections are opened and closed in total
quiz.explanation: The pool turns a burst into a queue: requests wait for a free connection and the database never sees more than the pool size. A higher limit only moves the ceiling, immediate retries add load, and closing later keeps connections open longer.

quiz.question: After a few hours, every request hangs. The pool reports 10 of 10 connections in use, but the database is idle. One code path throws an error after acquire(). What is the best fix?
options: Raise the pool size to 50, so that it takes longer before all the connections are in use
Restart the service every hour so that the pool starts again with free connections
Release the connection in a finally block (or a using block) on every path, including errors
Let the pool close connections that have been idle for a minute, so that it can create new ones
quiz.explanation: A connection that is never released is a leak, and an error path is the usual cause. Releasing in a finally block returns it every time. A bigger pool or a restart only delays the hang, and idle timeouts do not apply to connections that are marked in use.

quiz.question: Pooled connections keep their session settings. One request sets a user's time zone on its connection, and the next request, from a different user, sees dates in that time zone. What is the fix?
options: Give each user a dedicated pool so that settings never reach a different user's request
Reset the connection's state when it is released, or check it when it is acquired
Stop setting the time zone, and store all dates as plain text in the user's own format
Make the pool smaller, because fewer connections have less state that can be left behind
quiz.explanation: A pooled object is reused, so whatever state it keeps is lent out with it. Resetting on return, or validating on borrow, hands over a clean object each time. Per-user pools waste connections, and text dates and a smaller pool do not address the leak of state.
